utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Good morning, Mr. Mandic. I hope you had a good night, good sleep, good rest. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, yesterday you alluded to the personnel selection process in the MUP, and I understand that you could tell me many details about the manner in which that process angered Serbian officials as a result of certain actions by the SDA and by the Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you clarify that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Between the time of the election of the national parties and the ultimate split of the MUP, there was a process of installing personnel at various levels of the MUP, correct, and making selections of personnel to assume those positions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And there was considerable controversy and many tensions surrounding that process; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And on various occasions, you and members of the Bosnian Serb leadership expressed anger at the positions taken or actions taken by members of the SDA or Muslim officials within the MUP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Let me explain, Mr. Tieger, since you've explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'll certainly give you an opportunity to do that. But if I could just complete this process of questioning, and then to the extent further elaboration is required, certainly you'll be in a position to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I've been noticing that these questions are very leading, and I was wondering -- it seems that we're getting past preliminary issues now, and I would object, actually, to the leading nature of these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He's a Chamber witness, and the Prosecution is allowed to put leading questions, whatever impact it may have on the weight. That's the question I raised with you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I hadn't understood that the Chamber had actually made a decision that both parties would then be allowed to cross-examine the witness. But if that's your decision, that's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That's the way it follows, Mr. Robinson. Once a party has been called by the Court or Chamber, everyone else is entitled to cross-examine. It's not a question of us making that decision. It flows from the fact he's the Chamber's witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, the next question I wanted to ask was this: The fact is that all of the parties, the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ, attempted to ensure selections on the basis of ethnicity; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it also correct that all of the parties in power made unreasonable demands in connection with that process?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not correct. May I explain, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now you may explain, and I'll ask you further questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the winning parties who were in a collation, the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDA and the HDZ, at the republican level, at least as far as the Ministry of Police is concerned, had agreed about the distribution of senior posts. The first man in the police was to be a Muslim, the second man a Serb, and man number three was to be a Croat. And the same system applied in public security and in state security. As for districts and municipalities, it was agreed that in a district or a municipality where one ethnic community is in the majority, a member of that ethnic majority would be head of the police. A member of the second-largest community would be police commander, and the third ethnic community would provide the chief of the Crime Department. And that was the system in all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was not decided individually or differently in every municipality or district. It was a blanket principle. Did I make that clear, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think so, Mr. Mandic. And if the Court has any questions, they'll certainly inquire. The question I had asked you earlier was not about the over-arching principles or guide-lines for the selection of personnel, but instead about the actual implementation of that agreement. So when I asked you whether or not there was controversy or tensions involved in that, and you indicated, Yes, I understood that to be your indication that as the process went forward, there were conflicts surrounding the individual selections. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Tieger. And I can explain that using the example of the appointment of senior officials in the State Security Service. In that service, the post number 2 [as interpreted] belonged to a Croat, and the post number 2 belonged to the Serbs. In the meantime, the head of that service, with his associates, changed the staffing system and excluded the post that belonged to the Serbs, so that at the level of -- what had been agreed at the level of the republic was not implemented, as far as appointments were concerned. And that was one of the problems about which the Serbian Democratic Party complained and asked that the previous -- previously-agreed system be implemented with regards to appointments in the police. And that went on in certain districts where certain heads of security refused to implement the inter-party agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And all of the parties, in the context of the guide-lines you've just explained, were interested in ensuring that the personnel that they wanted in place were, in fact, put in place; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the personnel of other parties. I know about the personnel from the SDS and the Serb community. I know that since Vito Zepinic was man number 1 in the ministry from the Serbian community, I know it was the position of the SDS that really professional people, career policemen, be appointed to senior posts. I was never a member of the party and that was my case, and I wasn't even politically active. I got that post because I was 15 years a policeman, I was a judge of the Regular Court, I was an active sportsman; and, for instance, I met Mr. Karadzic only in 1991, when I was nominated for that position. Before that, I didn't even know about his existence. And it was at the insistence of Vito Zepinic that I got that post, and the assistance of my own brother, who was a teacher at the school in Vraca. And I can say with all certainty that all the personnel, at least as far as the Serbian community is concerned, were career policemen who had until then occupied various posts in the Ministry of the Interior and the State Security Service. And as far as I know, there was not one man who was recruited from the ranks of civilians or from other services to work in the Ministry of Police. And I'm only talking about Serbs on the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, notwithstanding the background you've just explained, and your own personal background, Mr. Mandic, I want to get to the bottom line on the nature of the process that took place from the elections until the split of the MUP. And in that connection, I wanted to ask you about something you said in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case. And in that case, at page 9453, you said the following: "The parties in power had very unreasonable demands of us in places where no Muslim was the top man. A Muslim had to be appointed at all costs, at the demand of the SDA. The SDS did the same. They insisted on appointments of their own people."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, and that's what I'm trying to explain. The SDS on several occasions protested in writing and asked that their personnel be appointed to those posts that were assigned to them by the inter-party agreement. And I believe that in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case, the letter of Mr. Karadzic was shown, a letter which asks that the inter-party agreement concerning appointments be observed. The chief of police was to be a Muslim. The chief of personnel was also to be a Muslim. And these two men were able to do or not to do whatever they wanted, as far as appointments are concerned, and all that was left to us was to insist that the inter-party coalition agreement be honoured.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. The transcript says "the chief of police was to be a Muslim," and the witness actually said "the chief was a Muslim."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm, Mr. Mandic, that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the chief of personnel was from the Muslim community, with the proviso that in autumn 1991, they replaced the chief of that service, but his replacement was also a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Let's continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the national parties in power identified particular persons whom they wanted to assume particular posts and pushed for the appointment of those people; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Tieger. Let me explain. The rule was that the ruling parties from the district that the appoints an individual nominate three candidates who meet the formal requirements; a university degree, no criminal record, et cetera, the basic requirements for someone to be admitted into the police. Out of these three nominations, we in the ministry decided who of the three would be selected. Let me give you an example. In Foca district, the man number 1 in the police went to the representatives of the Muslim community. People from Foca, from the SDA, sent three nominations. Mr. Hasan Cengic insisted that it be one of his relatives, Cengic, who graduated from medresa. We appointed Hilmo Selimovic, who was a career policeman. And then there occurred protests, and Mr. Cengic started sending me letters that I'm not appointing Muslims, that I'm interfering with the personnel policy, et cetera. This Hilmo Selimovic is now the first policeman in the canton, and I, in agreement with other representatives of both the Muslim and the Serb community and the ministry, made a decision on that appointment to avoid a controversy among the personnel in the police and in the SDA party. And this is the way in which we dealt with the maximalist demands of various parties, and we deflected them. And until then, there was harmony within the ranks of the police, until a different man came to the Personnel Service.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a remark to make about the transcript. About the word "medresa," there should be recorded that he was -- the man was a "hodja," which is a Muslim cleric.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, Mr. Mandic is speaking much too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 15, 14 and 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. When you would like to intervene, Mr. Karadzic, please put a pause, because both the witness and you are speaking the same language. Wait for the translation to be concluded. And the interpreters noted that you are speaking a little bit fast, Mr. Mandic. Please bear that in mind. Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tieger, I know that -- that's what I'm trying to say, there were maximalist demands, and that happened with the SDS at certain times and with the SDA and the HDZ. I don't mean the narrow circle of leadership. I mean party leaders on the local level, in districts where, for the most part, individual party leaders were pushing their own people to various positions. I gave you the example of Foca, where I made the appointment with the agreement with the then chief of personnel, Hilmo Selimovic, Minister Delimustafic, and Bruno Stojic. I appointed Hilmo Selimovic, who was a policeman with long years of service and who is now policeman number 1 in Sarajevo instead of a man who was a "hodja," a relative of one of the leaders of the SDA. I think I can still find this man's letters and complaints in my archives. His name was Cengic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you mentioned both the broader circle of the SDS, SDA and HDZ and the narrow circle of leadership involved in this process. The fact is that -- I'm sorry, you were nodding, Yes. The fact is that Dr. Karadzic got quite involved in this process; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as appointments in the police are concerned, no. For a while, Vito Zepinic made all the decisions about that, or, rather, Rajko Dukic, and then I took over that role of the personnel man number 1 in the police, and you have to believe me if I say that Mr. Karadzic never gave me a call saying, Mandic, go ahead and appoint this and that man. There were calls from various party leaders in districts and municipalities. Why? Because Mr. Dukic, who was the chief of personnel, had agreed at republic level which posts would belong to which parties, or, rather, ethnic communities; the Serbian, the Muslim, and the Croat communities. And Dr. Karadzic insisted that this agreement that had been signed be honoured. And in two or three places, this was never done, up to the end of the war, the post of the chief of police in Sarajevo, the post of the chief of security, and one other post. I can't remember which. There was pressure on us from the local level, from districts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let me draw your attention to something you said in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case, and that was at pages 9654 through 55 of that transcript: "Dr. Karadzic liked to meddle in these cadre problems. He always wanted to have a finger in the pie." First of all, Mr. Mandic, is that an accurate reflection of what you said?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Mr. Tieger, that you might have taken that out of context. Would you tell me what kind of personnel we were talking about? What was that relating to? Was it about personnel at republic level or all personnel at the level of municipalities and districts included.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Mandic, you tell me what aspects of the cadre problems Dr. Karadzic liked to meddle in.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like a clarification of what you just quoted. What was that discussion about? Was it personnel within politics, or the police force --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just suggest that we read out that portion entirely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which page, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 9654.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you have the transcript in front of you. It's 9654 through 9655 of the Stanisic/Zupljanin testimony. And I can read it out for you or you can -- I see you have documents in front of you. Maybe you have it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since the Chamber has not the transcript before us, if you could read out the relevant passage, if you find it necessary, Mr. Tieger, for the benefit of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The question related to the second half of 1991, and the question was: "So after you held the meetings and tried to resolve that within your own house first, after that you wrote a letter to the Presidency and the government and the Presidential Commission for the Protection of the Constitutional Order, that is to say, all the relevant institutions, you wrote to all of them and pointed out the irregularities and unlawfulness of the work of the MUP?" And you said that was your duty, all you were doing was your job. And then the question was: "And, finally, due to the fact that your letters did not bear fruit, letters to the top state institutions did not bring any results, you addressed the public in September and then again in February and so forth, and in your addresses to the public you were joined by the Serbian Democratic Party or Dr. Karadzic; is that right?" And then you said: "Yes, Dr. Karadzic liked to meddle in these cadre problems. He always wanted to have a finger in the pie."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I ask you to explain the nature of the cadre problems that Dr. Karadzic liked to meddle in.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably meant that he was meddling in an attempt to support us in our insistence that the personnel policy be honoured, because Dr. Karadzic politely asked several times the minister of police and the coalition partners that the coalition agreement be honoured at the level of the republic. That means that the executive posts that were to be given to Serbs should be given to Serbs. As for other aspects of meddling with that policy, I can say with full responsibility that Dr. Karadzic never interfered, nor did he ever ask for individual people to be given individual posts, but he insisted that Nedjo Vlaski, who was elected to become head of state security, be given that appointment, and that was the way in which he meddled, if that is called meddling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we can look at a few conversations that you had with Dr. Karadzic during that period of time. And I'd like to turn first to 65 ter 30113.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Tieger, for our reference, do you by any chance have the 65 ter number for his transcript in the Zupljanin case, Stanisic/Zupljanin case? Do you have that in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't believe it's up-loaded yet, Your Honour. We can do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Just for my information. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, while we're waiting for the document, observe that a finger in the pie is probably an English idiom, and it is probably not a good translation of what the witness actually said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's the subject -- proper subject you can deal with during your cross-examination. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. 65 ter 30113 is a conversation between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Mandic on the 22nd of July, 1991, and perhaps we can play a portion of that. And, Your Honour, I would also -- for the sake of expediency, perhaps it would be useful to provide the witness with a binder that contains the transcripts of any intercepts we may play for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, we'll play this for the Court and for you now, and you'll find the transcript at tab 1 of the binder that was just presented to you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Is it the office of Mandic? "Yes, is Mandic there, please?" "Yes. Who is speaking?" "Radovan Karadzic." "Just a moment, please." "Hello." "Good afternoon." "Doctor, it is Slavko, Draskovic." "How are you?" "Fine, thank you." "Did you do anything today?" "We gathered, compensating for some things." "I see." "Regarding Cedo, we just ... Momo went to see me and we'll probably finalise it quickly. And regarding other things, Mico is here and so on." "I see, fine. Push it, don't let it happen. Don't give up one man." "We won't, but we'll have to ... just a moment, Doctor, Momo would like to talk to you." "Okay." "Just a moment, Bye." "Have a nice day." "Thank you." "How are things, Momo?" "Well, President, I took power, and you can do whatever pleases you." "Sure, sure, who doesn't know how to take power shouldn't have it at all." "I have, I have already appointed myself and you can do whatever you want." "You just take it." "I'm joking. I went this morning to see Alija Delimustafic. "Okay." "And I told him that we had a meeting last night and that the party concluded that Cedo Kljajic cannot be replaced without agreement of the Serbian Democratic Party." "Not a one ..." "That is our personnel." "... personnel, not a one person can be appointed without our agreement." "We had a meeting today and Alija saw ... so I told him: Alija, please, let's not create problems and ... another MUP and so. And Alija agreed. We agreed to meet today with Hilmo, Alija, Osman Jasarevic in order to solve the Kljajic case. I told them: If he did something, it is lack of discipline. You should explain your arguments and we shall appoint a new Serb who is regular, who respects the rules and so on. If there are no grounds, you cannot replace him. You cannot do anything without the party." "Yes, yes." "And I told him that Dr. Karadzic sent his regards and that the SDA cannot appoint Serbian personnel. Fine, Momo, he said. In general, he agreed to finalise the matter today and I think that Cedo Kljajic will keep the position." "Okay. "He said: So Vito accepted? And I said, no, Vito. What do you mean Vito? You know that the party does not ... him any more ... he said, in that sense, immediately, immediately, President ... even minister does not want anything to do with him. Immediately." "Yes, yes." "He changed the story immediately." "Yes, yes." "Like, he blew it, this, that, in that sense and so on." "Yes, yes." "I called Jasarevic to stop everything. I have the decisions." "Fine." "I'm dictating this to Radmila, and I'm going to take it to Simovic and Krajisnik." "Okay." "That thing, our conclusion from last night." "When Hilmo comes there, tell him not to play games, because none of them would come out clean and unaffected. Everybody's career will be questioned if you fuck up with Serbian personnel." "President, Alija just told Hilmo that I would hear from him today. I ... and when I finish this." "Yes." "Because they blame now Mico Stanisic for -- they worked over the weekend. Avdo Hebib established a group concerning some guns. However it is all according to the law, legal and everything." "I see." "Because Mico Stanisic gave some arms to SUP, SUP Ilidza, Pale, and CSB. They thought it was civilian but it was not. Everything is regular, everything is according to the law." "Yes, yes." "The committee has been formed, but Stanisic was not informed. That is all. You know the structure of the committee." "Tell them not to play games because they will go to hell." "Mico and myself went to see Avdo Hebib. We made some trouble there and Alija got down to earth. He said, all right, Momo, finish that business with arms and Kljajic case. So you know that I have been working all this time." "Fine. Do you have any information ... They appointed a man in Prijedor on Friday afternoon. There is a Muslim commander. There now, a Muslim mayor and Muslim Chief of Defence, Territorial Defence." "I don't know, I will check it." "They want Miskovic. He was retired, but he is a young man. He could be active again." "Miskovic." Yes, they say he is all right. I've met him in ..." "Okay." "... right person." "Fine, President, I will do it now. Prijedor is it?" "Yes, Prijedor." "And that is our position?" "Yes, the position of commander is ours." "Yes, they appointed the mayor. They should have appointed the commander immediately so he can take up his duties at the same time; isn't that so?" "In Prijedor. Slavko in Prijedor." "Miskovic. I don't know his name." "Fine. Miskovic has not been appointed. Slavko says that he is. He thinks that he has been." "I see. But look at this, they fucked up something in Drvar. They appointed certain Maksic who is no good and the party does not support him. There it should be Zoran Srdic and Kunjadic, and not ..." "Srdic." "But, President, I don't think they have appropriate education level, but I'll check. Titov Drvar?" "One hasn't got one, one has." "Just a moment." "I think this one has one. But don't appoint Maksic, for God's sake. If he has to be appointed, let it be there." "Okay. "Because he is stopping everything and it wouldn't be good if he was there." "I see." "Because he was there until now and he is involved with old personnel and in knavery and everything. So, he should not be appointed." "Fine. Fine, President. That old guy, what's his name? "Old Maksic, he's no good." "Maksic." "He is no good. Cross him out." "Fine." "Kunjadic and Zoran Srdic are good ones." "Good, good, President, we will sort it out with Slavko, since it's a police matter." "Okay." "We'll do it today." "To appoint some Pecanac? "No." "No." "Not our personnel." "Yes, yes." "No problem." "Our personnel will go." "Fine." "Okay, President." "Thanks a lot." "We will inform you." "We'll be in touch." "Have a nice day." "Just be hard on them." "Cheers." "Whenever you're right, be hard on them. There is no other solution." "Have a nice day." "Cheers."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Mandic, I take it you recognise the voices in that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's Mr. Karadzic, myself, and Slavko Draskovic, who was deputy chief of police. Mr. Tieger, what we heard just now confirms my assertions; namely, that it was from the local level that pressure was exerted to have certain persons appointed. They even did that through Dr. Karadzic. How could Dr. Karadzic know of a person from Drvar, whether he is good or not, if someone from the party from the district had not called him and asked him to tell us? As for this Cedo Kljajic, secondly, we insisted, because he was a policeman for many years, that he remain in that position, but he did not suit some of the Muslim people who were in the police. It seems to me that you can see in this conversation that the local party chiefs exerted pressure to appoint individuals to particular positions, whereas I insisted that they should meet the formal requirements; that they should have university degrees, that they should not have a criminal record, that they meet all the formal requirements for these jobs. And I think that you can see that on the basis of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Mandic, and I wasn't suggesting that Mr. Karadzic knew, from the moment he assumed the position of president of the SDS, every potential candidate in every municipality without checking. So as you've indicated, local officials would be in contact with Dr. Karadzic and he would relate -- put pressure on him, is what you said, and he would relate to you who the candidates should be?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He just received these suggestions from these local people. But for the most part, we observed what had been set out at the very beginning, what kind of personnel policy was established in the MUP; that it should be longstanding policemen; that he should have a university degree; and that he was fit for that position. Dr. Karadzic never told me something like, That person does not meet the formal requirements, he's a criminal, or, He does not have the right kind of degree, but nevertheless appoint him to that position. No. I think, at least as far as I'm concerned, that I was rather independent, but of course I did honour my own associates and other people from the party; say Rajko Dukic. As for Radovan -- I beg your pardon, Dr. Karadzic, no, I think only as far as the most important posts are concerned that the leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party was interested in.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Intervention of the transcript. Page 17, line 20. The witness said he would forward it, and here it says "received suggestions," whereas these suggestions were forwarded from the local people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, is it correct you said you forwarded the suggestions from these local people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not me. President Karadzic would forward to me suggestions and requests made by party leaders at local level. President Karadzic -- well, I mean, I knew. It wasn't that President Karadzic was doing this personally. He didn't know these people. These were suggestions and pressures that were coming from the local level of various political leaders that I knew about, and I never understood this to be personal pressure on the part of Mr. Karadzic for particular jobs. It was a forwarding of proposals from local level that -- proposals that were made by certain leaders of the Serb Democratic Party at local level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, are you suggesting that Mr. Karadzic did not insist that the SDS nominations for positions to which it thought it was entitled, and which Dr. Karadzic thought the SDS was entitled to, were not honoured and were not implemented?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat that question? I'm sorry. I'm not exactly concentrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Wasn't Dr. Karadzic insistent that the SDS nominees to the positions that Dr. Karadzic believed the SDS was entitled to actually be implemented and those people be put in place?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, Dr. Karadzic did that when there were several interventions, when the inter-party agreement was not being honoured, and when we, in the police, at the level of the Ministry of the Police, could not carry this through, then we asked the head of the party, the leadership of the party, to have this resolved at the level of the presidents of the ruling parties, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, Mr. Radovan Karadzic, and Mr. Mate Boban, because these were crucial positions, key positions, in the police. Karadzic intervened only when we, within the police, were not able to resolve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Gavrilovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did I pronounce it correctly, Gavrilovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is such a surname, yes, Gavrilovic, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was he nominated to an important post?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What was his first name, this Gavrilovic person?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't have that post -- this first name. Did you know a man named Bojic, or Tomic, who were appointed to positions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomic is a frequent surname among the Serbian people, so I don't know who it is, whereas Zivko Bojic is a friend of mine from school who was head of the Crime Prevention Service in Banja Luka. That's that Zivko Bojic. There are quite a few people who have the same surname and who are not related in spite of that. I cannot remember any other Bojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's turn to 65 ter 30165. That's a conversation on the 26th of August, 1991. You'll find that at tab 2, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Who is speaking?" "Radovan Karadzic." "Good afternoon, Mr. President." "What are you up to?" "I'm in the meeting. There are some problems with Srebrenica, commanders, et cetera." "It was not only a problem with Srebrenica but also with Gavrilovic. Who has made that decision to replace him? We decided to appoint him to the position of that guy who retired, but nothing is getting done. What are these people thinking of? Who made Bojic candidate for inspector? Who appointed Tomic? Can that Selimovic give answers to certain questions?" "President, I would like to see you to discuss this. We need to agree and I would then pass on your views." "Listen, tell them immediately, if they don't correct these things, we shall ... appointments that are all nominations and appointments that are basically political functions within one week." "Yes." "That is basic and feel free to tell this to Selimovic." "Okay." "All nominations are political issues. All nominations come from the parties, and they cannot appoint one single person without our approval." "Okay, President." "Tell them. Tell them now." "Fine." "That we will consider him to be directly responsible. This will all pass, as well as criminal prosecutions, and we will make a list of people that will be criminally prosecuted, whoever fucks with us." "President, I will immediately with ... sit down and that." "And please tell that Gavrilovic was moved from the position of inspector for traffic violations. We nominated him instead of that one who left, who left, who was retired." "Up there as instructor?" "That Milan Buntic." "Milan Buntic?" "Yes." "Yes." "We nominated Gavrilovic for his position. We are replacing him. That means that anyone coming from the SDS is being replaced, like we are denouncing people. When we give support to someone they ... him ..." "Yes, yes." "As if we are not in power, fuck them. What do you think they are doing and how long they intend to act that way?" "President, we will finish it all." "I will see Izetbegovic today. I will tell Izetbegovic exactly what I mean, and it become public soon. When it comes to Selimovic and everyone in SUP who is fucking with us, I guarantee they will be criminally prosecuted." "Fine, President, I will remain with Selimovic and discuss everything." "Tell him severely that it is enough of that and I will request to terminate all appointments and to nominate people that SDS ..." "We'll see about Gavrilovic, Tomic, and that one there ..." "I don't want to hear about Tomic. Tomic is not our candidate in any case." "I know he isn't, President, I know he isn't. We will appoint our man, President." "Okay, and I will see that Cedo is appointed to the position that is appropriate for him." "I talked about that with Hilmo that Cedo should take the place of Obrad here ..." "Markovic." "Markovic." "Okay, I see." "We basically agreed about all of that." "Fine, fine. And if they want and if Selimovic and Hebib intend to live their life peacefully and have careers, they should be careful about what they do." "I will today ..." "Fine." "I will try to finish with Selimovic and I will inform you." "I will be at 5.00 at the Deputy's Club." "Okay." "If you can ..." "Fine, President." "I will go soon." "Okay, President. Hilmo Selimovic says hello." "Thank you. Say hello to him and tell him all of this." "Fine. "In a sharp manner." "Okay, President, have a nice day." "I will let you know." "Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I may make one suggestion or an option for the Court, and that is it is possible to listen to the actual conversation on the B/C/S channel and follow the transcript on screen. You may be doing that already, but I wanted to alert you to that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, again, I take it you recognise the participants in that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Mr. Karadzic and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'll ask you again. Who was Gavrilovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, believe me. I don't know who any of these people are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, how often were you in contact with Dr. Karadzic in connection with these personnel or cadre matters?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as telephone contacts are concerned, you have all of those telephone conversations, because Munir Alibabic listened to me from beginning to end and he handed it all over to you. So you have all of those telephone conversations. As for actual meetings, if something was difficult, complicated, sometimes I'd go to see him, but that was very seldom. As for these -- well, I repeat once again, Mr. Tieger, when we could not resolve problems, then we turned to the heads of parties on the one side or the other, or the third, for that matter. These were probably some complaints that went yet again through certain individuals, the heads of regional parties, who complained to Dr. Karadzic, and then he intervened with me to have all of this accommodated and to have professional people appointed to posts from the territories where these regional and municipal leaders wanted particular people in particular positions. I think that that was the problem. These were the maximalist requests put by all political parties, and that is what it has to do with. It doesn't have to do with the top, the center, the republican level, but the municipal and regional levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, before we go too far, I should have tendered those -- both those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you haven't tendered the previous one, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I should stand corrected, but is it not the first time that we are hearing evidence of one of the participants in the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, Your Honour. I know previously we've been MFI'ing the intercepts, but I think in this case it false within the guide-lines for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I recall the Chamber's ruling that when we decided to mark for identification all those intercepts, we said the authenticity and reliability of intercepts should be established by further evidence, such as hearing from the relevant intercept operators or the participants in the intercepted conversation, themselves. So unless there's a challenge from the Defence as to the legality or something else, if the witness confirms the content of the intercept, i.e., that such conversation -- if he confirms such a conversation took place, the Chamber is minded to admit the intercepts. Do you like to comment on that, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We would ask that they be excluded under Rule 95. We accept that with respect to Rule 89, the foundation has been laid for intercept evidence, but nevertheless these particular intercepts were before the war, and as I understand it, it was illegal -- they were illegally intercepted. And, therefore, under Rule 95, it's our position not to admit them in this Tribunal, where we try to maintain the highest standards of international justice, that it would be antithetical to the interests of justice to admit illegally-intercepted conversations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just add something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think so at this time. Mr. Robinson and Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber is of the view the Chamber will benefit from having a submission in writing from you. In the meantime, we'll mark those intercepts for identification. And no doubt the Prosecution will have an opportunity to respond to the submission from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We certainly will, Your Honour. This matter has been raised repeatedly in this institution, and the Tribunal has ruled on it repeatedly and consistently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll give an MFI number to those intercepts, 113 and 165.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter 30113 will be MFI P1079, and 65 ter 30165 will be MFI P1080.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I -- may I just say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that, and I state that once again. I do not recall the individuals that were being discussed here. I do not remember this conversation, but I did recognise my own voice and that of Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I want to turn next to a conversation which is 65 ter 30291. That's found at tab 3 of your binder. That took place on the 30th of September, 1991. And I wanted to play that in connection with the question of how regularly you were in contact with Dr. Karadzic in connection with these matters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Good afternoon." "Good afternoon." "Mr. Karadzic, please. Deputy minister calling." "Good afternoon." "Dr. Karadzic?" "One moment, please, deputy Mandic is on the line." "Thank you." "Hello." "Hello." "Yes." "Good afternoon, Mr. President, how are you?" "Very well, thank you." "Well, I don't know what, we called on Friday and finished it." "I was in Belgrade on Friday, Mr. President." "Aha." "Went to visit my son." "And where is he?" "He's at the military academy up there." "Ah, nice. Is he well?" "Excellent. A bit homesick, he only just left, so I had to go, he was crying a bit and so on, but it will be okay." "Aha, aha." "Away from home, from his mother and so on." "Aha, yes, yes. How long, when did he leave?" "Well, some 10 or 15 days ago." "Ah, he's in his first year then is he?" "First year, yes, yes, military academy." "Are you in your own office or with this guy, Selimovic?" "Yes." "With him? "Yes, yes." "Let me tell you, well I sent these guys for that job to be definitely done." "And regarding, who did you agree with Mr. President, regarding that?" "Hebib said ..." "Hebib." "For me to give five names to ..." "Very well." "To get a job over there at the fifth Administration where Vlaski was." "Aha, where Vlaski was, five of them is it ..." "Five, yes, because the SDA has, he said until, until, I don't know what now, I would like you to do that so that he doesn't, some gratitude, but anyway that is my basis." "Well, I'll get Hilmo, will do that, if Hebib agreed with you then there are no problems." "And shall I tell them that, I think you have, you have all of their documentation there except for one more. You have four sets of documents there." "Four is it? Get it for the last one and let them come and see me." "Okay." "During the day, Mr. President." "During the day." "Let them come see me." "Agreed. Otherwise, anything else new?" "Well, nothing really, no problems or anything." "Aha, okay, agreed." "Did you receive that Mr. President?" "Regarding?" "What Slavko brought you, the papers and such, the stuff I was asking you about the other day." "I think he did, I think he did, but I'm not sure, I think he did." "Aha." "I think he did." "Okay." "Okay. Now we have to be in touch almost daily." "Very well, Mr. President." "Agreed." "Talk to you later." "Have a nice day." "Cheers."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Mandic, do you recognise the participants in that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, this conversation took place on the 30th of September, 1991. I take it there was a lot going on at that time in connection with personnel selection, and Dr. Karadzic asked you to be in touch almost daily?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at that time we were already behind with filling vacancies, and that was becoming a problem in the Ministry of the Police. If we know that early that year we took these jobs and we were about to make personnel changes and reforms within two or three months, and we were already in September, we were already six months behind with the appointments, and it was becoming a problem already at the level of the whole Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was appointed in late September/early October, and the personnel changes and the appointment of appropriate people in appropriate positions had not been completed, and that was a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would tender that to be marked for identification at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P1081, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you mentioned, during the course of this morning, various maximalist demands, unreasonable demands, and so on, emanating from the national parties. At some point, did you raise the issue or suggest the possibility before your MUP colleagues of arresting both Dr. Karadzic and Izetbegovic in order to forestall ethnic tensions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was just before the war, when, at a meeting of the professional collegium, Mr. Alija Delimustafic said at one point, Let's arrest our bosses, Mr. Izetbegovic, Radovan Karadzic, and Mate Boban. But he insisted on Karadzic and Izetbegovic. And then, Between us, we will resolve all these problems in peace. Of course, that was not possible even, because Mr. Izetbegovic was the elected president, head of state. The police couldn't arrest him. But they could arrest Mr. Karadzic. And that was just a conversation, thinking aloud, between me and Alija Delimustafic, knowing that we must do something, because we could no longer stand all that pressure and all that was going on in the police, in the Ministry of the Interior. It was said more in jest than seriously, because in effect, under the law, we did not have the right to arrest the head of state. But I know that after that meeting, people ran to Alija Izetbegovic to tell him that as a joke, and some sychophants from among the Serbs went to see Karadzic and tell him, Look, these people and Alija Delimustafic want to arrest you. Of course, that was not serious. I knew very well what was possible and what was not, and we didn't mean it, of course. But that there were suggestions like that, yes, it was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you spoke yesterday about the dispatch that you sent on the 31st of March, 1992, splitting the MUP. I wanted to ask you some questions, relatively briefly, I hope, about the backdrop to the sending of that dispatch. First of all, let me turn your attention to 65 ter 00217, and those are the minutes of the first meeting of the Ministerial Council of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was held on the 11th of January, 1992. And I believe you had an opportunity to see and discuss that document during the course of your Krajisnik testimony. Do you see that document in front of you now, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to set the backdrop to that document: You recall the establishment of the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 24th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was established, but I was not there at the Assembly at the time. I know it was established on that date, but I did not participate in that founding session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the establishment of the Bosnian Serb Assembly was a response to the declaration in the Bosnian Assembly, the Joint Assembly, concerning independence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure. I was not a part of that, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at -- and one more question, and that is that: Following the establishment of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, the Council of Ministers was established, and you were aware of that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read that in the Serbian Gazette 1/92, the gazette of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And looking at the minutes of the first meeting of the Ministerial Council on 11 January 1992, and turning to the second page in English, and if we could also change the B/C/S page for the witness's benefit, if you look at item number 2, "Execution of tasks resulting from the declaration of the promulgation of the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And, Mr. Mandic, you were aware that on January 9th, the Assembly declared the promulgation of the Republic of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, the republic was declared?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I'm not sure. I did not participate in that. I'm a witness here, and I'm going to tell only about things that I know for sure. When I'm called here as an expert, then I'll explain this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Looking at the second paragraph under that item, that is, the execution of tasks resulting from the declaration, it states: "It was concluded that the priorities springing from the declaration included the defining of ethnic territory, establishment of government organs in the territory, and the economic disempowerment of the current authorities in the Socialist Republic of BH," that is, Bosnia-Herzegovina. And, Mr. Mandic, I bring this to your attention because at a meeting you attended on the 11th of February, 1992, in Banja Luka, the position of the Council of Ministers was raised. And if I could draw your attention to 65 ter 05413. And, Your Honour, with respect to the previous document, that's an associated exhibit. I can tender it now or it can come in along with the other exhibits associated with the previously-admitted 92 ter, as the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber hasn't discussed how to deal with those associated exhibits, given that he's now a Chamber witness. But in the meantime, I would like you to tender as you deal with them, in the course of your --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Then I do tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P1082, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something? I was not able to have admitted a single document if the witness did not know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I took it that you are of the opinion that all those minutes should be admitted. The Chamber will discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do you like to reply to Mr. Karadzic's intervention?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take this to be, and I assume I'm going to receive an affirmation to this, that this is more in the nature of Dr. Karadzic expressing some dissatisfaction with the responses to his previous submissions. I understood the Defence on repeated occasions to be encouraging the admission of all such documents, as the Court has noted. And, in fact, there was if not a joint submission, a mutual submission, much earlier with respect to such documents, beginning with the Assembly records, and then discussing other forms of official contemporaneous documentation. I'm confident these are records that the Defence has asserted to the Prosecution repeatedly it wants to have admitted. I don't think they've resiled from that position. So as I understand it, this is more in the nature of some observation about the admission of the documents he tendered, rather than the admissibility of this particular document or documents of this type. This document should be admitted. I would have laid a much more elaborate foundation if there was any reason to think that the Defence position was otherwise. We're going to spend a lot of unnecessary time, as Mr. Robinson, himself, has previously noted, if there isn't a consensus about the admission of contemporaneous official records of this type.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. However, the Chamber finds that the consistency is a great important factor, to be consistent with our previous practice. We'll mark it for identification, so that Exhibit P1082 is marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may say so, Mr. Tieger is right, it's a question of principle, not of substance. Of course, the documents that Republika Srpska produced are not going to be disputed by us, but I'm talking about the principle. I was not able to have admitted even documents that the witnesses were aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your point has been taken, Mr. Karadzic. Let's continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, have you in front of you now the minutes of a meeting held in Banja Luka on the 11th of February, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You attended that meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at that meeting, Mr. Stanisic raised, for the benefit of those in attendance, the position of the Council of Ministers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there a question, or should I give a comment, or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I'm asking to you confirm that at that meeting, Mr. Stanisic informed those present about the decisions of the Ministerial Council and the position of the Ministerial Council.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can see that from the first sentence, where Stanisic says that in the Socialist Republic of BH, the territory under the Serbian control, that control must be felt. I don't know what control he's talking about, when at that time it was still a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina. I can't understand this sentence uttered by Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Mr. Stanisic explained at the meeting, did he not, that work was to be done on the organisation of a Serbian MUP, starting with municipal and regional branches and working up to a Serbian ministry, itself?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we look at the conclusions of that meeting on the last page or second-to-last page in English. That's page 4, and for the B/C/S it will be the previous page. And, in fact, one more page back, beginning at Conclusions 1 through 5. Thank you. And that indicates, among other things, that: "The Serbian Collegium, the SR BH MUP, is instructed to carry out all preparations necessary for the functioning of the Serbian MUP after the promulgation of the Serbian Republic of BH Constitution. " That's conclusion number 3. And conclusion number 5: "Not a single decision regarding staffing policies in the SR BH MUP will be implemented without the approval of Deputy Minister Momcilo Mandic ." And just for clarification, Mr. Mandic, when there's a reference to SR BH MUP in this document, is that a reference to the joint MUP, and when there's a reference to the Serbian MUP, is that a reference to the anticipated Bosnian Serb MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. But this part, regarding the SR BH MUP, that's the joint MUP, for sure. Because I mention this assistant minister. That means it's a reference to the joint MUP. Where did you see the Serbian MUP? There's a reference only to the Serbian collegium. Within the joint MUP, a collegium was established including only Serbian members, Serbian staff members. In item 1, item 7, 5, there are references to a collegium of Serb staff members in the joint MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Conclusion number 3, the last four words of which are "Srpska Republika, BiH," and "Srpska MUP" previous to that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the adoption of the Constitution of the Serbian Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina. After the adoption of the Constitution, that's probably what was meant. Once formal requirements are met for the establishment of the Serbian MUP, that should be done, and that was done on the 31st of March, 1992, after the Law on Internal Affairs of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina came into effect. And I explained that in great detail in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And item number 18, finally, of the conclusions, if we could look quickly at that. And that was to inform the Council of Ministers of the conclusions of this meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I didn't ask you this previously, Mr. Mandic, but this was a meeting attended by all leading -- well, virtually all leading members of the -- Serbian members of the joint MUP at that time; correct? Yourself, Mr. Stanisic, Mr. Kljajic, Mr. Draskovic, Mr. Zupljanin, Mr. Bjelosevic, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Mandic, when you ultimately sent the dispatch on the 31st of March splitting the MUP --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I did not send a dispatch on the division of the MUP. I sent a dispatch on the establishment of the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you sent that dispatch, that was at reflection of the decisions of the Assembly in establishing the Constitution and the Law on Internal Affairs and the decisions of the Council of Ministers; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, and all that is written in the dispatch that I sent, all the legal grounds and instructions. And everything is correctly stated in that enactment, in that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in doing so, you were acting on instructions from the political leadership of the Serb people; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I acted following by the decisions of the Assembly, the Law on Internal Affairs, and the Cutileiro Plan adopted in Lisbon, the so-called Sarajevo Agreement. The political leadership at that time was not aware of that dispatch. They were somewhere abroad in Europe, attending negotiations. But since the legal requirements had been met, that is, eight days had elapsed from the publication of the Law on Internal Affairs in the "Official Gazette," and I was informed of that by Minister Velibor Ostojic, the legal requirements for sending that dispatch, in other words, the establishment of the Serbian MUP had been met.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it was the culmination of the process you've just spoken about; the meeting of February 11th, the Council of Ministers, the establishment of the Assembly, the declaration of the promulgation of the state, the Constitution, and the Law on Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting in Banja Luka was more a reflection -- an expression of discontent with the work in the joint MUP, not so much the establishment of the Serbian MUP. Many of the 15 conclusions talk about the shortcomings of the work in the joint MUP. Demands are made for everything to be done legally and legitimately, and only a couple of conclusions talk about the establishment of the Serbian MUP. The professional -- the hand of the professional collegium was forced, in a way. All these steps were dictated by something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time. I don't know what time the Court wishes to break, but I was a little late yesterday and I don't wish to be so today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I should have informed the parties that unless there's some objection from the parties, we are minded to in a somewhat extended form, so we are minded to have three 90-minute sessions today as well, if the biorhythm of the accused can bear with it. So the first session to 10.30. The second session will be from 11.00 to 12.30. The third session, after having some 45 minutes' break due to some circumstances of the Chamber, the third session will be from quarter past 1.00 to quarter to 3.00. So we have five more minutes, Mr. Tieger. If you have some problems --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be extremely helpful to know in advance in future. I have something I would need to change. I will endeavour to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll find out. What time would you like to conclude for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, at the moment I would have to conclude at 2.00, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 2.00. Okay, we'll bear that in mind. Let's continue until 10.30, and the Chamber will come up with a suggestion. Thank you for your information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before Mr. Tieger begins, can I just say something? We have sent a submission concerning the time when the Defence will commence its cross-examination. We are concerned that these changes might give us even less time for preparing our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll consider the matter as well. I see the time. We'll have a break now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, excuse me. During the break, can I go to my hotel room to take a pill for my stomach?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As long as you come back in half an hour, I see no problem, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ten minutes, ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I hope the Victims and Witnesses Section can deal with it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, before you resume with the questioning of Mr. Mandic, the Chamber would like to go back to the intercepts that were played in court this morning. Having been played in court and discussed with the witness, the accused objected to their admission on the basis that they were obtained before the war, and thus illegally. As a result, the Chamber decided to mark it for identification, the intercepts, as Exhibit P1079 and MFI P1080 -- I'm sorry, and MFI P1081, until such time as it made a ruling on the accused's submission concerning legality. However, in making this decision, the Chamber, mainly myself, overlooked the fact that it has already ruled on this issue in its decision on the Prosecution's first motion for judicial notice of documentary evidence, dated 31st March 2010. That ruling can be found in paragraph 10 of the decision, and provides that the admission of intercepts into evidence does not depend on whether they were obtained legally or illegally. Rather, the Chamber must simply be satisfied that the requirements for admissibility of evidence, provided by Rule 89, are met, and that there are no grounds for exclusion under Rule 95. The Chamber, therefore, reconsiders its earlier decision to MFI the relevant intercepts, and instead, given that the witness is one of the participants in the conversation played, finds that all the requirements of Rule 89 have been met in relation to them. Accordingly, these intercepts should be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I apologise. I also overlooked that decision. I'll go back and look at it now. And if for some reason we don't feel we've made all the arguments under Rule 95 that we would like to, we can make a written submission, but we understand now. I'll go back and look at that, and I apologise for not bringing that to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Robinson. And as to the Defence motion for an extension of time before he starts the cross-examination, Mr. Tieger, I would like to hear from you, if possible, at the end of today's session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And as for the scheduling for today, we'll sit until -- for this second session, we'll sit until 12.30, and the third session will be just 1.00 to 2.00. Let's continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I want to turn next to some issues that were raised during the course of your testimony in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case. And in that connection, I'd like to turn next to D88, and that's English page 60 and B/C/S page 75. And I want to -- I'll be showing you a portion of a speech by Mr. Vojo Kupresanin that you were shown during the course of your Stanisic/Zupljanin testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, have we dealt with the exhibit you dealt with previously before we adjourned?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Perhaps not, Your Honour, and my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted, unless there's any objection from the Defence. Yes, they will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 05413 will be Exhibit P1083.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 75, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you were read out a portion of what Mr. Kupresanin said on that occasion, and it was: "I am against any kind of joint institution with Muslims and Croats. I personally consider them to be our natural enemies. You already know what natural enemies are, and we can never again live together. We can never again do anything together." And you were asked whether you heard others, apart from Mr. Kupresanin, expressing such sentiments in the period of time before the outbreak of the conflict, and your answer was -- sorry, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please go ahead, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And your answer was: "I've been listening to the same things from 1990 until 2010."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this thing with Mr. Kupresanin, this session. I did not attend that Assembly session when Mr. Kupresanin said this. I think that it had to do with the appointment of some personnel in the field of the judiciary, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, if you'll focus on my question, Mr. Mandic. At page 9443 of the Stanisic/Zupljanin transcript, the excerpt I just read out to you was provided and read out at that time, and the reason was because you were then asked whether you had heard others, apart from him, express such sentiments. So the issue was not -- the issue was the focus on the expression about natural enemies and living together, rather than your attendance at that particular session.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 9443? Is it the Krajisnik case or the Stanisic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Stanisic case. In any event, Mr. Mandic, is hearing that excerpt read out, "I personally consider them to be natural enemies, you already know what natural enemies are, and we can never live together," is it correct that you'd been listening to such sentiments from 1990 until 2010?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please read out my answer? I cannot recall that detail in relation to that Assembly meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Q. Now, did you hear others, apart from Mr. Kupresanin, express these kinds of sentiments? "A. Are you referring to the period before the war, during the war, or after the war? "Q. I'm referring to the period before the conflict broke out in April 1992. "A. I'd been listening to the same things from 1990 until 2010." And I'll continue because it's relevant: "Yes. At the moment, I'm concerned with whether these sort of sentiments were expressed by others in the government or in the Assembly, apart from Mr. Kupresanin." And your answer, Mr. Mandic: "Believe me, Madam Prosecutor, that there were other people who were playing on the Serbian card and trying to ingratiate themselves to Karadzic and others. After that, they would go with their Muslim and Croat brothers and have coffee."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's my opinion, yes. I confirm what I said there to Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at page 9523, you also testified that there were people in the Assembly who wanted a mono-ethnic state, and you identified some of them; Mr. Brdjanin, Mr. Prstojevic, Mr. Milojevic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you mentioned, during the course of your testimony as well, that Prstojevic was another who sought to ingratiate himself with Mr. Karadzic through the expression of such sentiments. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was trying to ingratiate himself with Mr. Krajisnik, rather than Mr. Karadzic, because he was deputy and represented Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, is it fair to say he would have been trying to ingratiate himself with the Bosnian Serb leadership, including Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Mr. Krajisnik only, that he was trying to ingratiate himself to him, because he was the deputy and the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in any event, Mr. Mandic, I want to ask you about some of those people you spoke about, some of their positions, and some of their interactions or discussions about or connections with the Bosnian Serb leadership. First of all, let me ask you about Mr. Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know Mr. Kupresanin at all. I never communicated with him, I never talked to him. I think that he was president or some high official in the SAO Krajina. I just saw him a few times at some Assembly sessions that I attended. I don't know anything about the man. I know that he was one of the right-wing persons that we are discussing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And my interest in asking you about -- my focus in asking you about Mr. Kupresanin is not about the depth of your knowledge about Mr. Kupresanin, but about your indication earlier that the sentiments he was expressing were those that you were familiar with from others in the Assembly or in other positions of authority. First --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, these right-wing sentiments or, rather, the Serb nationalism, it was expressed in the Assembly, where some people, like this Kupresanin, whom I really don't know - perhaps I saw him about twice ever in my life at these Assembly sessions - and this came to expression at Assembly sessions. After these Assembly sessions of the Serbian people, or the Joint Assembly, they would go and have coffee with those same people that they had spoken out against, that is, Muslims and Croats. That did happen. I viewed that from the side, viewing it as a person from government, from the police. Now, were they trying to ingratiate themselves with the people in this way? Were they trying to ingratiate themselves with the president of the Assembly or the president of Republika Srpska? That, I really don't know. But, anyway, it seemed like false nationalism to me. It was aimed at the public, as it were. That was how I experienced it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Mr. Kupresanin was a member of the SDS Main Board?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know anything about the man, really. He's from Krajina, Banja Luka. I don't know anything about him. I just know the people from Sarajevo and from around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you were correct that he had a position of authority in the SAO Krajina. He was the SAO Krajina Assembly president.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he held a high position in the SAO Krajina, but I didn't know which one. And I know that at these sessions, these assemblies, he represented the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned the expressions at the Assembly sessions. Let me ask you to look at some examples of that, if we may. If we could turn to D84; in English, page 26, and B/C/S, page 41. And here we see Mr. Kupresanin speaking again, talking first about the vast territories where Serb municipalities are possible in the region, and the need to annex those territories. And if we turn to -- leave it on the same page in English, and turn to page 42 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUPRESANIN SAYS
utterances.text: "Why are we doing this? "I personally think that our living space and the territory in which we live and work is endangered, and we have to avert that danger. Actually, we have to prevent Muslims from moving into our territories and regions." Mr. Mandic, is that another example of the kind of sentiment you heard expressed in the Assembly and elsewhere --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness does not know Vojo Kupresanin, and he cannot speculate about what Vojo Kupresanin was thinking. I was never allowed any such thing, not anything close to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really cannot analyse now what Mr. Kupresanin was thinking and what he was saying. I really don't know the man. I did not attend these sessions. I am a witness here. I'm not an expert. I cannot analyse his psyche and his attitude towards other peoples. I really don't know the man, and I cannot analyse him now through these sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic was able to answer the question in general terms, although he didn't know, personally, Mr. Kupresanin. So he may answer the question, if possible, in general terms again, as to the general sentiment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said to Mr. Tieger, and I repeat that once again, and I said it in the Stanisic case, among the ranks of deputies, among the Serbian people in the Joint Assembly, and in the Serbian Assembly, too, there were some right-wing persons, nationalists, who advocated, well, a state of the Serb people without other peoples and such-like. But it seems to me that that kind of thing can happen in any country in the world, any nation in the world, any assembly in the world. There was nothing unusual there, nothing that had never happened before or has not happened since. It really didn't say anything special to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Mandic, my -- with that understanding, I'm interested in knowing from you the -- we know that Mr. Kupresanin said this, and I'm interested in knowing from you whether you heard such sentiments expressed by others during the period 1991-1992; that is, that living space was endangered, that danger has to be averted, and that Muslims have to be prevented from moving into Serb territories.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember, Mr. Tieger, that anyone had said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you were completely unfamiliar with such a sentiment; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, that's an unfair analysis. He didn't say he was completely unfamiliar with such a sentiment. He said that he couldn't remember anybody actually saying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate that, Your Honour, and maybe that question should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, apart from your inability at the moment to recall a specific occasion or a specific person who said that, were you familiar with that position among deputies of the Assembly, or members of the government, or municipality representatives, during the period 1991/1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among the members of the government, as far as I can remember, there weren't any. As for the members of the Assembly or, rather, other bodies, that is to say, Assembly, government, the executive, the legislative, I am saying once again I cannot remember whether there were other such people like Vojo Kupresanin.
