This does not seem to be something that I remember, and I cannot state anything in that regard. However, I'm sure that as for the government -- as for official meetings of the government, such a tone was never used, and nothing like that was said about other peoples living in Bosnia-Herzegovina while I was in government.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to some of the positions of the government at a later stage, but I'm still interested in exploring with you the kinds of sentiments that were expressed at Assembly sessions; not only generally, but specifically by some of the people you mentioned during the course of your Stanisic/Zupljanin testimony. If we could --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you give me an example, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. If we could turn to 65 ter 00039.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for the record, this has been admitted as Exhibit P921.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And page 77 in the English, page 53 in the B/C/S, please. This is an Assembly session of 8 January 1993, and once again this is Mr. Kupresanin - we'll turn to some of the others shortly - saying: "We say that the war was not necessary in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The war in Bosnia and Herzegovina was necessary. Right now, if we were to count the population right now, there would be over," and I believe in B/C/S that may be "around a million Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bosnia and Herzegovina would be predominantly a Serb republic. Is war necessary in Serbia? It's a horrible thing to say that the war would be necessary in Serbia. If Serbia does not go into the war now, then in three to five years the Albanians and Muslims will entirely legally overtake the power in Belgrade, along with the Serb opposition. This war was necessary for the Serb people."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, did you hear others express the view that the demographic change, affected by the war and the reduction in the Muslim population, was necessary for the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking for my opinion. First of all, let me explain to you, Mr. Tieger, that this session took place in 1993, when I lived and worked in Belgrade. I repeat, I don't know the man, I don't know Vojo Kupresanin. I can't remember anybody saying anything to that effect. I've never seen these words before, the ones that you have just shown me. These are not nationalist words. These are fascist words. I don't have a comment. I don't know what you want me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just want to you answer the question, Mr. Mandic. Did you hear others say that; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember ever having heard anything of the kind. I really don't remember, I don't remember at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you to look at one more remark by Mr. Kupresanin, specifically. And I want to turn to some others, but I'd you to look at remarks by Mr. Kupresanin at a rally. That's 65 ter 04234.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'd like to interpose a relevancy objection here. If we were trying Tony Blair, for example, would something someone had said in the House of Commons during some debate be relevant at all to what Mr. Blair had acted or what he had thought? And I think this is basically the same thing. There are extremists in every government and every assembly, and how does it really advance the Prosecution's case to show to this witness or ask him to comment on comments like that in the trial of Dr. Karadzic. So I would ask that this line of questioning be ruled to be irrelevant and to lack probative value. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, we're at the beginning of hearing this witness's evidence, we're at the beginning of hearing evidence about what was said in the Assembly, we're at the beginning of hearing evidence with respect to the relationship between the persons who expressed those views, other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership, and Dr. Karadzic. And, first of all, it's premature in that regard, and I will be showing -- presenting some -- and I'm happy to present some documents indicating that and fleshing that out generally. But to take these comments in the abstract at this moment, before the Court has an opportunity to see the extent to which they were expressed, the reactions to those expressions, the interaction with the people who expressed them and the leadership, is, as I would indicate, premature and prevents the Court from receiving the evidence it needs to hear. And in addition, this is precisely the manner I understood that the Court wished to hear such evidence. We talked about the submission of Assembly sessions in their entirety, and we still wish the Court to hear that, and we'll be in a position to, at that point, identify for the Court, with greater detail and with more clarity, the inter-relations I spoke about and the significance of these comments. So there is value, we submit, to the Court having the opportunity to review these things. This witness has indicated under oath and in an earlier case that he heard expressions, at least, of the desire for a mono-ethnic state by multiple people in the Assembly. I think the Court deserves an opportunity to hear some of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for future purposes: Mr. Mandic, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can understand more than I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger and Mr. Robinson, although Mr. Mandic did not know Mr. Kupresanin at the time, but I take it Mr. Tieger was exploring the possibility whether there were instances Mr. Mandic heard at the time as to the general circumstances, but then maybe the question that has been put and answered several times, and it's more appropriate to concentrate on the specific cases where Mr. Mandic was present, so with this answer I would like you to move on to other instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, before I do, Your Honour, if I may, I indicated to you we wanted to present to the Court some of the instances of the inter-relations and of linkage of the people mentioned to the Bosnian Serb leadership, and I'd like to explore a couple of those documents now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Tieger, to interrupt, but it's plain that this witness's speculative comments on matters which may be hearsay, if that is the effect of asking him questions about people he didn't know or meetings that he didn't attend, it's -- I speak for myself, but it must be evident to anybody that the probative value of that is extremely small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I wanted next to turn to 65 ter 30116. Mr. Mandic, I want to play a portion of this. This is at, I believe, tab 2 of your binder of intercepts, and I'll be asking you about some portions of those. It's a conversation that took place on the 23rd of July, 1991. And if we could play a portion of that for Mr. Mandic and ask him if he recognises the voices on the intercept.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "And you are?" "Vojo Kupresanin." "Oh, it's you, Vojo. I don't hear as well because of the TV. Just a second. I'll get Radovan for you." "Hello." "Good evening. Hi, President." "Good evening, Vojo. What's up?" "Well, I was in --" "You were?" "I was in the neighbourhood." "M'mm-hmm." "And someone told me that you needed me, so I called you." "M'mm-hmm." "Was there some -- a meeting today in Dubica?" "Well, I was in Srbac today, along with five municipalities of ours regarding the Savo situation and that --" "M'mm-hmm." "We analysed the economic situation and problems as well as assistance and the creation of staff. But they were in Dubica last night, well as far as I know, I wasn't there. Well, actually, I wasn't invited at all, I heard that Brdo and Grahovac were there." "M'mm-hmm." "And that they were with Babic." "M'mm-hmm." "And that the Party President Vukic was there." "M'mm-hmm." "They made some kind of agreement, regarding the referendum. I heard it today. I also heard that a similar meeting, on that issue, at the level of the Krajina Assembly would be held in Banja Luka on Friday at approximately 3.00. Actually, one would be at 3.00 and the other one would be later, around 5.00 or 6.00, in the community centre also, but in the bigger hall." "What referendum, referendum about what?" "Referendum about Krajina. That's what I heard today." "Are they fucking nuts?" "So, what do you suggest for us to do?" "I beg you, Jovo, don't do things that you could be arrested for. We're not entitled to violate the Constitution, we will now start negotiations with the Muslims. Today, we had two meetings with them about the historical agreement between the Serbs and the Muslims to maintain Yugoslavia. And that, such things are happening here too and the police here are informed about it and the Muslims are angry. We are negotiating with them to keep Bosnia in Yugoslavia to connect SAO Krajina to Bosnia, to Bosanska Krajina, and you over there are doing such things and destroying every political action we take." "Well, it's good if it's like that. It's okay, can I have contact with you tomorrow?" "Please, a meeting of the Main Board is on Thursday. On Thursday, we will finally clarify if that's the party that makes us over there, whether those people that belong to the party that conducts such a policy or if it's some other party. We have to clarify this. I can't do my job if somebody unauthorised does some things somewhere. That is an unauthorised act. That couldn't be done without the Main Board. What were they thinking?" "You know, I would suggest that all the participants in the Main Board be present. "All of them. Well, they are all obliged to come because the executive committee is to be formed. They should all be there, they should all come, too, because we want to issue an epistle, which is, we are making steps that will most certainly create the best possible results for us. And to listen to Milan Babic, who only runs around without asking anyone. Maybe he thinks he's the smartest person in the world?" "So, my suggestion was the following: Brdjanin, who is not a member of the Main Board, as well as Grahovac, who is also not a member of the Main Board should come to that session of the Main Board." "Let them come." "But that mistake, that kind of mistake, could that be fatal for all of us? "That was fatal, man! At the first session, they will vote for the termination of mandates and arrest all of you. We may not be able to say anything. They even prepared complete documentation to show it to John Major in England and to Mitterrand in France with all the evidence that the Serbs are creating the greater Serbia, and now you're playing right into their hands, as if they're paying you. Fuck, man." "Okay." "That's incredible to me. Does someone over there think he is smarter than our political council? We are not splitting up. We had a meeting last night too." "Okay." "We are analysing, asking, asking a child, asking a great academic, we are working normally and then some fools show up making premature steps. "That will happen, Vojo, but they have to be responsible for that." "Okay." "They have to make a mistake. They will definitely make a mistake. We know that." "So shall I call you tomorrow?" "Yes, call me, please, and make sure everyone is at the Main Board --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I stopped that prematurely. If we can just continue for another minute.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "-- the Main Board meeting on Thursday. They have to be responsible and disciplined towards their party or otherwise I will come there and create a new party and new officials. Because, that's not the way it should be. That's irresponsible and could cause a catastrophe for the Serbian people." "Okay." "What the fuck else am I supposed to do? Who created that fucking regionalisation? Did I secretly influence you and produce documents where we determined what you were to do? The one who wants to be born after seven months instead of nine months, will hardly survive. They want to create some kind of premature child and miss this chance forever. Fuck, they are getting involved in this, like Tudjman is paying them." "Okay. I will then talk about this tomorrow, very serious -- tell them they're not authorised to make shit within this institution, that they have to form another party to do that. And that I will come to Bosanska Krajina and discredit them in front of the people. As long as this the Serbian Democratic Party, it's more difficult for me to deal with our people than our opponents. Fucking shit, is it normal that it's harder for me with our people? Are they all wethers or people? Politics is not run like that. You are not to follow your wishes, but you are to set up an option, and then you make a move in order to be a certain winner. Instead of keeping your plans on your forehead and then you play into other people's hands." "We had a meeting today in Srbac, and we made an agreement that this would be our mutual position, but I think of Belgrade, I think of Sarajevo, that's what I think of. And that we all agree on what to do and where to go. I mean, we also don't have a whole lot of information. Maybe we are not supposed to have those pieces of information." "Vojo, I have said: Now we have to create a structure of the region, realistic structure, which means that we are to form the Culture Fund and SDK Public Auditing Service. So all the money should go through one SDK, the Krajina SDK. So, these kinds of realistic moves, we are not making any spectacular political moves, until they make a mistake, because we do everything within the Constitution. Milan Babic didn't form the SAO Krajina before Croatia changed the Constitution and violated their obligation towards the Serbs." "Yes, yes." "So we have to wait for them to violate the Constitution. When they do that, we have everything prepared. I will meet tomorrow and I will tell them what you have just told me and I'll let you know tomorrow and the day after about how everything goes." "Yes, please. And please be responsible towards politics, even children wouldn't --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please switch off your microphone. Otherwise, the interpreters cannot actually hear the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second -- is that what you said? Yes, thank you. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Yes, please. And please be responsible towards politics, even children wouldn't do such things." "Well, I wasn't there last night. I didn't avoid that but they didn't invite me. I don't know why. Today I have a meeting in Srbac and some people, who were there, Ivastanin was there and he told me what had happened. I told you what he had told me, and now you told me about the possible consequences and that's a very serious thing for me." "Yes, okay. So please call me soon and don't let any mistakes occur." "Okay." "And I see you at the Main Board on Thursday. "I will call you on your -- home number." "Okay. Call me late in the evening." "Okay." "Deal."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, when you said in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case that Mr. Kupresanin and others were trying to ingratiate themselves with members of the Bosnian Serb leadership through the expression of such sentiments, you were aware, weren't you, that Mr. Karadzic had extensive contact with leaders of the regions and the municipalities throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in particular the areas ultimately claimed by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of Karadzic's contacts with his political associates.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. Tieger implies that we wanted to appropriate our own territories. How can one appropriate territories where one has lived forever?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a matter for your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic. The witness has already answered the question. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I will not cross-examine Mr. Tieger, will I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you were aware, through your dealings with Mr. Karadzic in the context of personnel selections for the MUP, that he had extensive contacts with municipal leaders and regional leaders throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of his contacts, but I know in certain instances that some people, as I've already explained, used the party and the president of the party to impose some of their staff arrangements on the ground. Those were very rare instances, but you have all that documented in intercepts. And that happened in the second half of 1991, when major problems had occurred because the staff policies agreed in Bosnia-Herzegovina were not implemented, in terms of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to look at a rally and some speeches at that rally attended by a number of the people you mentioned and members of the Bosnian Serb leadership. And if we could turn to 65 ter 04234.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, would you like to mark for identification --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's 40 -- yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- the intercept?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P10841.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the document is 65 ter 40035.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in the previous intercept, Mr. Mandic, did you identify Mr. Karadzic's voice there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could stop that for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, as mentioned, this is a rally conducted on 21st of August, 1994. And do you recognise the person speaking on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see a TV reporter, and I can see a name, Predrag Radic. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. Let's continue with clip 2 of that, and we'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Are you watching a video-clip or watching a transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Video-clip. There's a TV reporter and there is Predrag Radic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it's difficult to understand why Mr. Mandic might have the beginning of the rally rather than the clip that is, I think, in front most of us at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I had difficulty how come he was seeing a name. Yes, he was watching it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we be given the exact 65 ter number? We're not sure that we have the exact number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you able to identify the person who is speaking there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The only person I can identify is one of the escorts to Mr. Karadzic. And I believe that this person with the moustache is Stojan Zupljanin, he looks like him. And the speaker, I don't know who that is. The man sporting a moustache is probably Stojan Zupljanin. And this person here is one of Mr. Karadzic's escorts. And I don't know the speaker, I don't know who that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's continue that excerpt. This is Mr. Kupresanin speaking, as we can see in transcript of the rally. Let's hear a portion of what he has to say.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "There's no Muslim state in the Serbian land, the land that has been ours forever. There is no Muslim people, and the entire world knows this."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Could we pause for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a major problem with the translation. He didn't say "there's no Muslim state." He said "there's no Islamic state." The difference is huge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be checked into later on by the CLSS, and with that caveat, we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "There are only Serbian people in these parts. There are Serbs who are Orthodox, Serbs who are Catholic, and Serbs who are Muslim. "Under 6, we must urgently determine Serbian territories and borders and present them to the Serbian people for their acceptance, because there is no state without a set territory, a territory demarcated and borders demarcated. Bosnia is an eternally Serbian land."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Show number 3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin, people's deputy." Mr. Tieger, switch off, please. [Voiceover] "Brothers and sisters, dear people of Krajina, and all other patriots who have come to this rally, we must not succumb to the greatest deceit that we are voting for war or peace. We are voting for the betrayal or rescue of Republika Srpska. Those leftist forces which are offering us co-existence again must know that it is the obligation of the Serbs over the next hundred years to wipe their feet from the foul non-Christians who have befouled this soil of ours."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I indicated to you that this was also attended by members of the Bosnian Serb leadership, including Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic. And let me turn quickly to their comments. Clip 4, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Momcilo Krajisnik, president of the Assembly of Republika Srpska." "Dear brothers and sisters, my dear people of the Krajina on both sides of the Una River. Having heard these wonderful words by my predecessors, I feel great satisfaction at being at this gathering here today, satisfaction at seeing the fruits of our struggle for our homeland in actuality."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And clip 5, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Our goal is that all this we are fighting for today becomes a united state. May God grant this. All the territory now called Republika Srpska or Serbian Krajina will be Serbia!"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And clip 6, which follows immediately afterwards. And, Your Honour, at the conclusion I'll present the time codes for the benefit of the record.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Brothers and sisters, president of Republika Srpska, Dr. Radovan Karadzic has the floor." "Dear brothers and sisters, Serbs from both Krajinas, from Herzegovina, from Posavina, from Ozren, from all Serbian lands to the Neretva River. Six hundred years have passed since we lost the Serbian state, and two hundred years Karadjordje's uprising to renew the state has lasted, and what is happening today is the conclusion of Karadjordje's rebellion. If Karadjordje had to stop at Dobrun, on the other side of the Drina, it was because he was unable to complete everything, but we must complete it. Our enemy has brought us to the most beautiful and most sacred goal of ours."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, when you mentioned Brdjanin as one of those people who wanted a mono-ethnic state, and when you talked about Kupresanin, it's the case, isn't it, that these two were not isolated extremists expressing marginalised views, but were, in fact, people embraced by, supported by, and connected to Dr. Karadzic and the rest of the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you weren't aware that Mr. Karadzic, for example -- Mr. Krajisnik, for example, as reflected here, supported and praised the words of Brdjanin and Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you put to me only excerpts taken out of the context of entire speeches. I'm not an analyst. I don't want to analyse the stances expressed in public places where large numbers of people had gathered and these people are trying to win over the masses and telling them what they think they want to hear. I'm not an analyst. I don't know when this gathering took place, where. I'm seeing this for the first time now on the screen. I can't now, based on three or four sentences taken out of entire speeches, confirm your view that they supported Kupresanin or Brdjanin or that they didn't. That was not my impression. I know that Momo Krajisnik, and especially Mr. Karadzic, while I was minister and assistant minister, did not advocate a Serbian state. I know that for a fact. But what they said at rallies for the benefit of the people, I don't know, and I don't want to comment on it. Out of a rally that must have lasted three or four hours, you took out a couple of sentences, and you want me to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you were aware that Mr. Brdjanin was an advocate of a mono-ethnic state. What did you hear him state that caused you to understand that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period do you mean; before the war, during the war, after the war? When? I don't understand. I didn't get your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, at the moment I'm not so interested in when Mr. Brdjanin's advocacy of a mono-ethnic state began. I'm interested in knowing the basis and how you knew that that was his position.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably attended some Assembly sessions where he expressed his views and his opinions, because I'm sure that Brdjanin was an MP in the Joint Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also in the Assembly of the Serbian people, and he was an MP from Krajina. He was one of those right-wing MPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I indicated I would list for the record the time codes of the clips that were played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Clip 2 is at 0:51:19 through 00:52:03. That was Mr. Kupresanin. Clip 3 with Brdjanin speaking is 00:53:32 to 00:54:41. Clip 4A, which was the beginning of Mr. Krajisnik's speech, is 1:10:07 to 1:10:37. And the second clip of Mr. Krajisnik is 1:26:09 through 1:26:29. And the last clip with Mr. Karadzic was 1:26:32 to 1:29:03.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I make a request? I believe it would be of assistance both to the Chamber and the Defence to know the date and the immediate reason for these rallies, because it must have had something to do with peace conferences, because there was a mention of something that needed to be accepted or not accepted. So it's important to know the date and the occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I noted it was 21st of August, 1994, at the beginning, and the reason for the rally is a proper subject for you to pursue during your examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, and I would tender the document in its entirety, along with the transcript, at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I just say a few words, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, for the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm advised, Mr. Tieger, that parts of this clip have been already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- admitted as P14, and there is a way that we can add the remaining parts to P14, following our previous practice. That will be done. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I would just point out that we believe that this comes outside of the guide-lines with respect to whether this witness could speak to any of those portions. And so while it may ultimately be admissible, we don't think it's admissible through this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's time for -- yes, I forgot that request. Yes, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've been trying to tell Mr. Tieger that in 1993/1994, I lived and worked in Belgrade, and I am not at all familiar with the political circumstances in Bosnia-Herzegovina, who was right-wing or not, where rallies were organised, and who participated in all these events. I think it's really superfluous for me to repeat that as far as these years are concerned, I can be of no use either to the OTP or the Defence or the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was too quick to give a ruling on my own. But upon second thought, the Chamber is of the opinion that although the witness identified some of the persons who gave a speech in the video-clip, but he said nothing about the content of the speeches, so to be consistent with our previous ruling we'll not admit these video-clips at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand the Court's ruling, and I'm not -- I want to seek some -- I wasn't heard on this, so if the Court will permit me to raise a point; if not for this purpose, then for future admissibility purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The authenticity of this document is not at issue, clearly. Furthermore, it involves the accused directly. It follows on the heels of testimony under oath by this witness in a previous case, confirmed here, about the general kinds of sentiments he heard and their -- what he perceived as they're being part of an effort to ingratiate the speaker with Dr. Karadzic or other members of the Bosnian Serb leadership. Now, the Prosecution is attempting to explore the kinds of sentiments that were expressed at that time, the reactions to those sentiments, the linkage between the proponents of those sentiments and the members of the Bosnian Serb leadership, and we'll be attempting to do that during the course of the case. It cannot be the case, and this is actually a point argued by Mr. Robinson earlier, that the Court would find it necessary to understand the significance of such evidence to ensure the presence of someone who was personally present at the time. Instead, when a document is relevant or -- and authentic as we -- excuse me, Your Honour. When a document is authentic, then the issue arises whether the context of the witness's testimony thereby makes that document and the discussion of that document relevant. And, again, so I'm not seen as revisiting a ruling the Court is making, I make those submissions as a general point, but that is the point I would have made if I had the opportunity or if I'd taken the opportunity earlier to speak to this document and other documents which we will be presenting during the course of this witness's testimony. These are of assistance to the Chamber, we submit, and hope the Chamber will hear them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Also bear in mind, in your future planning of your conduct of examination, please also bear in mind that the case we are dealing with is of great, enormous size, and we have to think about who will be -- although we do not adopt the so-called best-evidence rule, we have to think about who will be the best witness to produce certain exhibits, so we have to think about whether there's a point of putting documents or clips to the witness who knows nothing about the document. So otherwise there's no limit, also in terms of cross-examination or re-examination. That's the point. And I forgot something else, but let's move on with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. I understand --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Your Excellency, just briefly? Mr. Tieger omitted to quote the witness. The witness said: "To themselves with the leadership and the people," although you can argue that in some cases it's the leadership, but in this case, these video-clips, this is a political speech, and it would be ingratiating themselves with the people. And so that somehow was not highlighted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't think this is a proper, appropriate intervention on your part. That's -- those parts can be examined during your -- pursued during your cross-examination. Let's not waste time anymore. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This only referred to the words of esteemed Mr. Tieger, whom I'm not able to examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you have formed the habit to like to have the last word, but please refrain from doing so, Mr. Karadzic. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you mentioned more than once that you weren't sufficiently familiar with Mr. Kupresanin or Mr. Brdjanin. Let me ask you about somebody that I understand you dealt with directly, and that's Mr. Prstojevic. Now, he's another one of those who you said wanted a mono-ethnic state; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider him as a right-wing MP, both in the Joint Parliament and the Assembly of the Serbian people. I know him from Ilidza, because he was also president of that municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I want to look at how Mr. Prstojevic happened to be in that position of power and retained that position of power in Ilidza. And in that connection, I wish to turn to 65 ter 20992. Mr. Mandic, that's a discussion between you and Mr. Lugonja on the 17th of April, 1992, which you reviewed and authenticated during the course of your Krajisnik testimony. I'm sorry, did I -- it's 65 ter 30667. My apologies. And, again, Mr. Mandic, it's found at tab 10 of your binder of intercepts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Hello, good morning." "Good morning." "Petar Lugonja needs to speak to Momcilo Mandic, please." "One moment." "Hello." "Hello." "Hi, Petar." "Momo, hi there." "Hi Pero. What are you up to?" "Here I am. How's it going?" "It's fucking all right. How about you?" "Well, fuck. Problems, huh." "It's fucking shitty. I wanted to ask you." "What's up?" "Lugonja: Well, I fucking have these three people here in Ilidza. Tomo is pulling to his side because he's from the police. I believe that he's -- that he's mainly right. Then there's Prstojevic, the president of the party and the Crisis Staff, and then there's Kezunovic, the prime minister, you know." "Yeah. It seems that this Kezunovic guy is in some way right most of the time, but Prstojevic is -- he seems to be gathering some kind of scum around himself, some incapable, incompetent people. Does anyone at this moment have the influence to calm this thing down, to find a fourth person who can fucking unite all this?" "Well, I'll call Prstojevic to come in and I'll talk to him here." "Yes, but it's no fuckin' use. Kezunovic is from up there in Pale and he's a good guy. I guess he took his family up to Pale yesterday and the day before it. He also spoke to Karadzic about something, you know?" "Yes." "But a new man has to come here, one that can really unite us. "No, if there is discord, they can go fuck themselves, all of them. I'll fucking kill them all." "Come on, Pero, you are the smartest and the most able man there." "Well, it's impossible." "Koljevic came in last night. They shut themselves in and they won't let anyone in." "Well, yeah, they're running to the boss. All right, I'll talk to Koljevic." "Talk to him. There has been a split and it's been a mess in Ilidza since day one. Don't let us have this man -- he can't give any orders." "All right. I'll take care of mobilisation. We are unable to move people." "Is it possible to reach you there?" "It's possible." "Lugonja: It's possible, but --" "All right. I'll see when I have --" "When these guys get here quickly. It only matters to us that we have someone to get a fuckin' move on." "Agreed, agreed." "Right. Cheers, bye."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, when you listened to and explained that conversation in the Krajisnik case -- well, first of all, let me say that is a conversation between you and Mr. Lugonja; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you explained that conversation in the Krajisnik case, at page 8626 through 8627, you explained that Lugonja thought that Prstojevic was taking people who were not proper and were not behaving appropriately, that they were impeding the setting up of civilian authorities in Ilidza, and that's why he asked to have that problem resolved by President Karadzic. And you explained that there was a clash between Prstojevic and Lugonja; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then you further explained that as a consequence of that, Lugonja left Ilidza, whereas Prstojevic stayed on in Ilidza for a long, long time. So Prstojevic had this stream of his own, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a conflict at a local level. At least in this case, Petar Lugonja got the short end of it and went to live in Belgrade, whereas MP Prstojevic became president of Ilidza municipality, and he stayed in that position for a really long time. And we had more problems with him later, and you will see in that intercept between me and Tomo Kovac, when I even asked Tomo Kovac to intervene as chief of police with regard to Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you were asked why Mr. Prstojevic prevailed in this conflict for local authority, and you explained: "I think that the entire leadership of Republika Srpska had greater confidence in Mr. Prstojevic, and that's how it happened." So it wasn't only Mr. Krajisnik, but it was Mr. Karadzic, too, and Mr. Koljevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that, and I still think that, Mr. Krajisnik prevailed, in terms of trust in Mr. Prstojevic. It was his MP in the Assembly. And Momo Krajisnik was protective about members of Parliament and people he worked with in the Assembly, and he had more trust in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you've said that Mr. Prstojevic was one of those who favoured a mono-ethnic state. Let's take a look at a conversation involving Mr. Prstojevic at 65 ter 30746 to see what views he expressed at the time. And this is tab 14, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is this all about? Who is on trial here? What do I have to do with -- I mean, there are a million and a half Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Everyone was free to say what they liked. Mr. Tieger cannot -- can show any number of documents where people expressed extreme views. That's a matter of freedom. We have to work on the basis of documents, the Assembly, the government. Now, based on informal conversations between free men, who have the right to have extremist views, I am being painted in a certain light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't find this intervention very helpful to the Chamber, Mr. Karadzic. You can leave it to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it -- thank you, Your Honour, but perhaps it provides some context. Before we break, let me turn to another document quickly. That's 65 ter 00028, and it's the 17th Assembly session, which may already be admitted, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, you would like to tender that previous intercept?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 30667. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1085, Your Honours. For the record, 65 ter 00028 has been admitted as Exhibit D92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What page, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Page 66, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we have the date of an intercept, if that's an intercept ?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, it's not. It's an Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the page in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Same page in B/C/S. The problem may be that we're still in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this is the 17th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly in late July 1992. I believe you attended that session, spoke at that session. This is Mr. Prstojevic speaking, and I'll quote: "When the Serbs started the uprising in Sarajevo, and when they seized control over certain territories, there was no government, or at least it was not known where it was then. Moreover, we did not know -- we even did not know if Mr. Karadzic was alive during the first couple of days. When we learnt that he was alive, and when he visited us in Ilidza and encouraged us, the Serbs from Sarajevo retained control over the territory, and even extended their territory in some areas, driving the Muslims out of the territories where they had actually been majority." Mr. Mandic, is that another one of the comments you heard Mr. Prstojevic make during the course of your attendance at the Assembly or in dealings with him that caused you to understand that he was an advocate of a mono-ethnic state?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Prstojevic personally. And from my personal experience, I know that he was at right-wing extremist, that he spoke about a mono-ethnic Serbian state. He was a very opinionated person. That's my personal opinion of him, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The witness said "stubborn and opinionated."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stubborn and opinionated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stubborn and opinionated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He very often did not take into account the opinion of other people, of his own partners, the leadership. He was a negative personality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Before you rise, I just should note the Prosecution did file a response to the motion for extension of time, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We know. Thank you. We'll resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I was informed that you have something to raise before we -- yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, Your Honour, just in the event that -- we would like to have just one moment to reply to the Prosecution's position concerning our request for a delay in the commencement of the cross-examination of the witness. Would this be an appropriate time or would you prefer to do it at some other time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Once we've started, please do so, and very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to point out that in the decision that you made on the accused's motion for postponement of the trial on the 26th of February, 2010, at page 40, you indicated: "As the trial progresses should the accused make a reasonable request for more time to prepare his cross-examination of a particular witness or to deal with a particular document which the Prosecution seeks to introduce into evidence, on the basis that relevant material was only recently disclosed to him, the Chamber will consider such a request and may grant appropriate relief." And this is the time. We believe this falls squarely within that paragraph, and because of that, we think that the Chamber envisioned situations like this may occur, and this is one of those situations, given the volume of documents and the lateness of their disclosure to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll try to give a ruling as soon a possible, possibly tomorrow. Thank you. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't know it's a funny procedural anomaly at this moment. We filed a written response to the written submission. First of all, let me say that normally I think a reply shouldn't be assumed. It requires leave of Court when one is necessary. But what I'm trying to find out now is whether the Court still is seeking an oral submission at the end of the day. I would certainly dispute the basis for the reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary, and I think that Mr. Robinson's reply was in response to your written submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I agree, and I'm only trying to forestall the procedure whereby, because we're in court, that the normal formalities of written submissions gets circumvented simply because someone rises in court to make an oral submission in a situation that would otherwise provide for written submissions. I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's not spend more time. I gave permission. Let's continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, just before we recessed, we had an opportunity to look at some comments by Mr. Prstojevic at the 17th Assembly session, some retrospective comments about the period in April. Before that and before Mr. Karadzic's intervention, I had been -- I had intended to play an intercept involving Mr. Prstojevic, and I think that was almost lined up. And that would be 65 ter 30746.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can we have the date of the intercept, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That's 14 May 1992. And we need to be in Sanction for that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Hello, hello." "Yes." "Good evening." "God be with you." "How are you?" "It will be better. Tell me ..." "Prstojevic speaking. I'd like to talk to Mrki." "Mrki is not here. Mrki 2 is." "Okay, Mrki 2 then." "Just a second." "Yes?" "Prstojevic: Hello, hello." "Yes?" "Good evening." "Good evening." "How are you? Prstojevic speaking." "I'm Mika's deputy." "Yes, and your name is?" "Milenko." "Milenko?" "Yes." "Why did Mika phone me?" "Phoned you to check with you ... these people in Kotorac ..." "Yes." "What should we do with them?" "Did you arrest them? What did you do?" "People are down there. On -- just a second. Yes?" "Hello." "Yes?" "And where are those people? Have they been arrested?" "No." "What then?" "Down there on the road, all of them. Men are separated from women." "Ha." "Just a second, just a second." "Up there; right?" "He says men ... I've just received the word. Men are in the Kula Prison, and women went in the direction of Butmir." "Put Tepavcevic on." "Here, here's Novakovic. He'll talk to you. It's Prstojevic. Stop fooling around." "Hello?" "Hello?" "Hi, Neda." "Hi." "How are you?" "I'm fine. Have you been cleaning Kotorac today?" "They have. I don't know the exact details because I was engaged otherwise." "Yes." "Well, if you want, we will call you later." "That's okay. But tell me, please, I beg of you, why did you take the women to Butmir?" "They said women were not in Butmir, but --" "Nedeljko Prstojevic: But?" "Well, in Butmir, yes. Not to KP Dom, but to Butmir. That's where they are going." "They cannot go to Butmir, we'll mop up Butmir in time as well." "Aha." "Butmir will be mopped up, Sokolovic will be mopped up, Hrasnica will be mopped up." "Well, I don't know where to take them." "They will all ... there's is Bascarsija. Please, take all them to Bascarsija, on foot." "Aha, aha." "Women." "Okay, now I'll ..." "And men to prison." "Okay, I'll check with them now and then I'll let you know." "Yes. Tell them, those who convert to Orthodox religion on the spot, they can stay, women and children." "Aha, okay." "Do it, please, but don't make mistakes ... You've done an excellent job, but it means that Butmir will be mopped up in time. Tell that to the people here." "There you go. Cheers." "Okay."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, do you recognise the voices of any of the participants in that discussion?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, no. I don't know who Mrki is. Prstojevic -- I'm not sure, but I believe that one of the voices belongs to Prstojevic. And for the other man, I don't know either the name or the voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as I indicated to you, that is a conversation between Prstojevic, Milenko and Mr. Novakovic on the 14th of May, 1992. Is that the kind of information -- that is, what you listened to in that intercept, the kind of information you had about Mr. Prstojevic's activities back in April and May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prstojevic did not participate in those activities. He was the president of the municipality, but I believe that he interfered in the life of the municipality in everything; the work of the police, the military, and other institutions. But I've not heard this conversation before. I was never aware of these particular details. I was aware of some other incidents that he was involved in, and I discussed them with Tomo Kovac. While I provided my testimony in Belgrade and on the Krajisnik case, I heard those intercepts. You played them to me. That was when he had blocked Ilidza and then removed some Muslims from their jobs, and I, personally, and the government were against that. As to this particular intercept, I don't know anything about these particular activities, and this is the first time I hear this intercept at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Mr. Prstojevic was engaged in removing Muslims from Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the municipality, of the local parliament, as it were. He did not agree with the police, and I don't know what his relationship with the military was. But Tomo Kovac, as the head of the local police, did not approve his activities. At this time, or perhaps even before, I talked to Tomo Kovac, the head of police, about problems created by Prstojevic. He had blocked the movement of non-civilian population through Ilidza. You presented that intercept to me, if you will remember, Mr. Tieger, both in Belgrade and on the Momcilo Krajisnik trial. I don't know to what extent he was engaged. I don't know. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you said, in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case, that Mr. Prstojevic and his ilk were dangerous, and expressed your disapproval in that case of him, and also indicated that he was a proponent of a mono-ethnic state, weren't you talking about your awareness of his efforts to ensure that Muslims in Ilidza did not remain?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we be given the transcript page, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we be given the transcript page, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 9523, regarding a mono-ethnic state. 9505, regarding Prstojevic and his ilk and attempts to ingratiate. Also, 9487.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, when I paraphrased, I was asked to quote. Could Mr. Tieger actually quote from the transcript, and could he quote the entire paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Could you reformulate your question, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let me go back to the transcript, but first if we can short-cut that. You have a low opinion or you have expressed a low opinion of Mr. Prstojevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have a very high opinion of him, and you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And was that because of, despite, or had nothing to do with his views about a mono-ethnic state?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know Mr. Prstojevic privately, but I didn't agree with his methods of work in Ilidza municipality. Tomo Kovac, the head of the police in Ilidza, had informed me about those methods of work on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was asked to read a quote about Mr. Prstojevic from the transcript of the Stanisic/Zupljanin case. Let me read one and perhaps more. After quoting -- after you were presented with the same Assembly session excerpt we saw just before the recess, that is, Mr. Prstojevic speaking at the 17th Assembly session, about driving the Muslims out of territories where they'd actually been a majority, you were asked: "Now, that appears to be carrying along the same line from Mr. Karadzic was saying. You knew Mr. Prstojevic, and you rang him up to tell him to stop driving Muslims out. Had he actually taken any notice of what you'd said to him? "A. Well, I learned about those activities of his from Tomo Kovac a few days before, and in one intercept I even suggested to Kovac that he arrest or kill the man because he was creating problems to everyone in Ilidza, the authorities and the police. He was really destructive, and you see he was denying the existence of the government and that Mr. Karadzic was alive, et cetera. My opinion of Mr. Prstojevic and his ilk could not be worse. Those people created most of the problems, and many of them ended up here in The Hague." That was later clarified to be that they caused others to end up in The Hague. So, Mr. Mandic, you acknowledge here your awareness of Mr. Prstojevic's efforts, and my question is whether or not the contents of the intercept you listened to were consistent with the information you had at the time back in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger -- Mr. Tieger, I adhere by what I said in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case as regards Prstojevic, and there's an intercept of the 2nd of June, 1992, which shows that I tried to undertake measures. You presented it to me, and here I have it under tab 17 or 18. And you will hear that I'm trying to convince Prstojevic to behave within the scope of constitutional law and that the government had received information about his destructive behaviour, and I was imploring with him to stop with all that. One of the things was the complete blockade of Ilidza municipality and about Judge Fadil Musanovic who couldn't work because he was Muslim. I asked him to stop with all that and to bring the man back to work. As the minister of justice, I did not have any authority over him. I informed the government about all that. He was an elected president of the municipality, and he was responsible before the Parliament. You have that intercept, I have it here, on the 17 or 18, and you'll see that we did discuss his case, that we tried to do something, but he was not within the line of our responsibility and we could not take any effective measures with his regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 18 here, under tab 18, a conversation between Miljenko, Prstojevic and myself. For the Trial Chamber, could we perhaps play it so that the Trial Chamber could hear what I told him and how I reacted, how the government reacted? I reacted as a member of the government. I tried to persuade those people to come to their senses and not to behave in the way they did, under tab 18 of a binder you provided to me. The document number is 5747, pages 1 through 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No doubt Mr. Tieger will take care of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let me say, in terms of -- first of all, Mr. Mandic --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise. I would kindly ask you to allow us to hear this intercept of the conversation between myself and Prstojevic, and then everything will become clear. The relationship with the government and that man in Pale will become clear, because he did not enjoy the support of the government in what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just so the Court is clear on this:

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By "the government," Mr. Mandic, you mean the ministries headed by Mr. Djeric, that is, that arm of the political authorities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was a government member, and as the government, I intervened, and I asked from Prstojevic to behave as a good Serb, as a person who was not monolithic, who was removing people from their jobs because they were not Serbs. I asked that from him. And here we have the intercept, Mr. Tieger. Could you please play it for the Trial Chamber? I asked Prstojevic to behave within the Constitution and the law, as a good Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any -- first of all, I was about to say I don't have any objection, but that's not exactly the procedure in which we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I leave it to the parties. Either the Prosecution or the Defence will play the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Fine. I will simply note this is one of the associated exhibits. It's discussed at some length in the testimony that the Court now has in evidence, and that's the reason it wasn't replayed. And, Your Honour, I would tender, as MFI, the intercept just played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this a proper moment to tender that, when the witness confirmed nothing about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think in the context of his extensive answer, he talked about his knowledge of Prstojevic, Mr. Prstojevic's activities, and so on. Again, I don't -- he didn't authenticate the intercept in the classic manner, that is, by being a participant, but that's a separate matter, as we've discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification. Yes, that will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P1086, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I want to move on to some of the government's activities, because you've referred to them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even more important things I couldn't do. The witness didn't know anything about all that, nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Marking for identification has many implications. So when we are -- those will be admitted when we are satisfied with its foundation, in addition to the authenticity later on. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, and please understand I'm not trying to initiate a squabble with respect to this intercept, but it's an opportunity to address a general admissibility issue, and I think it's on -- and I don't want that also to be embedded when it comes time to mark -- to consider the admission of this document later. The witness knows one of the participants, he knows about his activities. We've already established the connection between that person speaking in the intercept and the accused in connection with the same activities that are part of that conversation, so I think it's inaccurate to suggest that there's been no nexus and this document has arisen from nowhere in the course of this examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I believe the parties will be aware of the Chamber's guide-line or Chamber's practice in relation to the admission of documents, and the Chamber will be consistent with that rule. And while it is still amazing that admissibility is such a hard issue, after the 17 years' existence of this Tribunal, let's move on, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I couldn't agree more, and maybe we'll have an opportunity to discuss that with the Court and with the parties at some -- in the near future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll see, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just say two things? One is a matter of principle, and so is the other, but also a practical thing. Could the Defence be asked every time for their opinion about a document tendered for admission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I apologise for that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I think we found out now that you're not a shrinking violet, and I'm sure that if we fail to remember you, you'll certainly remind us straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in particular, Mr. Mandic, I want to move to the period of April 1992, shortly after the outbreak of the conflict. And in that connection, I'd like to turn to 65 ter 00151. And, again, we may be in Sanction, and -- Mr. Mandic, this is -- this document reflects the minutes of the meeting of the Council for National Security, that is, the National Security Council, and the government, which was held on the 24th of April, 1992. Now, you were familiar with the National Security Council and, indeed, attended some meetings; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just attended one meeting, when I was proposed as minister of justice; not before, not after that. I think it was an ad hoc body, and it never actually went through the legal regulations of Republika Srpska. The proposal was that I replace Ranko Nikolic as minister of justice of the Serbian Republic -- yes, of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who presided over meetings of the National Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At page 8743 of the Krajisnik transcript, you were asked: "Q. Who presided over meetings of the council? "A. Dr. Radovan Karadzic." Is that correct, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at these minutes, Mr. Mandic. And if we look at the decisions following item 1, that is, the decisions listed, and turn to the third decision from the bottom of that section: "The National Security Council adopted the decision that the Ministry of Justice shall take over the exchange of prisoners once the organs of the interior have completed their work." You may not see that on your version of the B/C/S, Mr. Mandic. If the B/C/S could be moved to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I once again caution that the word used here is "zarobljenici" [phoen], not "zatforenjici" [phoen]. That can be confirmed by your interpreters. When it says "zarobljenici," it should be translated as "prisoners of war," "of war," because no one ever exchanged mere prisoners, but prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, I thank you for your intervention, Mr. Karadzic. In the future, if you'd like to intervene, could you raise your hand before you just speak out. Thank you. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, after this decision and this meeting, the government then passed a decision to establish a state commission for exchange; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, Mr. Tieger. Obviously, I did not attend this session. This is the first time I see this decision that this council - I don't know which body this is, anyway - passed a decision that the Ministry of Justice should deal with prisoners of war after the Ministry of Police. I just know that it was the government that made a decision to establish a central commission for the exchange of prisoners of war. I'm aware of that, and that was one of the first decisions of the government since it came into being. I think it was the first or second document of the Government of Republika Srpska, once it was established. So it wasn't the Ministry of Justice that ever established a commission for the exchange of prisoners of the war. It was the government. The government made this decision, not the Ministry of Justice, because on the 24th of April, Mr. Tieger, there was no Ministry of Justice in the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, a couple of things, Mr. Mandic. You just said that's the first time you've seen this document. If we look at page 8743 of the Krajisnik transcript, we see: "Mr. Mandic, P433, the documents before you now, are the minutes of the meeting of the Council for National Security and the government, held on 24th April 1992." And then before asking questions about the document, there was some discussion about your attendance of meeting of the National Security Council, who the members of the National Security Council were, who presided over meetings of the council, and then your attention was directed to the contents of the document, including the decisions and the decision that the Ministry of Justice shall take over the exchange of prisoners once the organs of the interior have completed their work.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I attended a particular meeting when I was proposed as minister of justice. I cannot remember that it was then, and I cannot remember this decision. I know that once I was informed -- or, rather, once the proposal was made to appoint me minister of justice, that was the end of April 1992, for a few days I carried out preparations to establish the Ministry of Justice. And it was only in the beginning of May, I think on the 12th, that I was appointed or elected minister of justice at the Banja Luka Assembly and when I took over the ministry. Up until then, it did not exist. Ranko Nikolic, who was on the Ministerial Council, was the first minister of justice, and people were waiting for the man to take over that duty, but he stayed in Sarajevo throughout the war. So from the Ministry of Police, I was transferred -- or, rather, I was informed the proposal was made that I would take over the Ministry of Justice because I used to work in regular courts as a judge in Sarajevo. I do not remember, but I know with certainty that it is the government that passed the decision to establish a central commission for the exchange of prisoners of war, and I cannot remember the name of the man now who was appointed to that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll look at that decision, Mr. Mandic. You were also asked: "Was the decision adopted on April 24th that the organs of the interior would investigate the captured or detained people, and then once the Ministry of Interior was completed, the Ministry of Justice would conduct the exchange of those people?" And you said: "After this meeting, the government passed the decision to establish a state commission." And then you continued to indicate who would be on that commission?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I repeat once again what I said a few moments ago, that the Ministry of Justice did not establish any commission. As for this decision, I really cannot comment upon it because I am not familiar with it. But I do know what happened in the government and in the Ministry of Justice during May and during the rest of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what kind of body this council was. Was it formal, was it informal, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Mandic, that you were shown this document when testifying in Mr. Krajisnik's case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I allow for that possibility, but I really do not recall. I was a witness for President Krajisnik in 2004, so six or seven years ago. I cannot say with any certainty. But if Mr. Tieger asserts that it was shown to me, there is no reason for me to deny that was certainly the case then. But at this point in time, I simply cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have before me that part of the transcript, and then you were shown exactly the same document as this, and you were asked: "First of all, were you present at the meeting at which that decision was adopted?" And then this was your answer: "I don't remember, but probably I was, although I don't remember." Which is different from your answer today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, Your Honour, I'm testifying under oath. I do not remember at all a meeting of the National Security Council. I know with certainty that I was invited to one such meeting, but only briefly, when personnel issues were being discussed and when the members of that council informed me that I had been proposed to become minister of justice. Now, whether I attended that part of the meeting or the entire meeting, I don't know. But I really do not remember this document and, therefore, cannot comment upon it. Believe me, I cannot. You know, when promotions were made of certain physical persons, then those persons would be invited to that particular part of the session. But when security issues were being discussed, then only the members of that council were present. Later on, it turned into the Supreme Command or whatever it was called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you can confirm again at this time of an NSC meeting with the government, the Ministry of Justice didn't exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. At that point in time, the Ministry of Justice did not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one final minor, minor question from me. As to your date of appointment as minister of justice, when Mr. Tieger yesterday summarised your testimony as to your date of your appointment as being May 19th, you corrected that to be May 12th --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the Assembly in Banja Luka. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At the end of the session, you said you were appointed the 16th of May. Which is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know -- or, rather, if my memory serves me well, on the 12th of May there was an Assembly meeting in Banja Luka, where I was appointed minister and where I took the oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to turn your attention to the document establishing the Exchange Commission. But before I do, in connection with its relationship to this meeting of the National Security Council, I'm going to draw your attention to page 8752 of your testimony in the Krajisnik case, where you were talking about the Commission for Exchange, and you said: "If I may, I would like to try and help you. "After this meeting of the National Security Council of the government, where the decision was taken that the Ministry of Justice would establish the Exchange Commission, after that a government session a state commission was formed involving various ministries." That's correct, isn't it, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't any ministries. There were people from individual ministries, but it was pre-war ministries, Mr. Tieger. And Rajko Colovic never worked for the Ministry of Justice of Republika Srpska. He was assistant minister for criminal sanctions in the joint government where Ranko Nikolic was minister, and, as such, he came to that commission; was elected, that is. So Colovic -- Rajko Colovic was never an employee of the Ministry of Justice, as far as I can remember, where I was minister, that is. He was assistant minister for the implementation of criminal sanctions in the joint government, and the minister was Ranko Nikolic, who was the first minister of justice of Republika Srpska or, rather, a member of the Ministerial Council that was established in January or December -- or, rather, January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just following the chronology, let's look quickly at 65 ter 11225. Oh, and, Your Honour, if the previous document hasn't been tendered, I would do so at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in essence, I have no objections, although the witness did not know anything about that meeting. However, I do not object to having this document admitted into evidence; from the point of view of authenticity, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness confirmed his attendance in one of the council meetings. And then given your position, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1087, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you'll see before you the 8 May 1992 decision to form a central commission. The heading is "Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Government," and it states in item 1: "Central Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War, arrested Persons, and the Bodies of Those Killed which remained in the opposite side, is hereby appointed." And it indicates the members of that commission, including Mr. Markovic, as representative of the Ministry of the Interior, Mr. Mihajlovic, as a representative of the Defence Ministry, and it says Rajko, representative of the Ministry of Justice, would be the president of the central commission, is that Rajko Colovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was Rajko Colovic, who was a member of the Ministry of Justice but in the joint government. As such, he was included in this commission, because you see, this is the second written document of the government. See, it is dated the 8th of May, and the number is 01-2. I was the first employee of the Ministry of Justice. I was appointed on the 8th of May. Or, rather, this document is from the 8th of May, and I was appointed on the 12th of May, and things intermingled and they did not move as smoothly as they do in peacetime. Rajko was appointed head of this commission before I became minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So this is one of the first things that the government did?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Obviously, this is the second document that was written up. It says "Number 01-2." From this text, it can be seen that it was done urgently, under pressure exerted by the international community and on the basis of what was happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the Exchange Commission was active almost immediately; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I didn't know about that. I cannot give an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll just look at 65 ter 01553, please.
